summary: The Independent feature looks at how people cope with insomnia in 2023, from kiwis and lavender to earplugs and masturbation, tied to the Apple TV+ comedy Still Up. Sleep therapist Dr Lindsay Browning explains that quick fixes often act like placebos and can exploit desperate sufferers, while Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBTI) is the gold-standard treatment. It also covers statistics on prevalence, the higher risk for women, and the NHS approval of the new drug Quviviq.
one_line: A look at insomnia hacks, their limits, and evidence-based treatments like CBTI, framed around Apple TV+'s Still Up and expert Dr Lindsay Browning.
key_facts: Globally, around 10 per cent of adults are estimated to meet the criteria for insomnia, defined by difficulty falling or staying asleep to the point of disturbing daytime functioning.

Studies have found women are 40 per cent more likely to be affected by insomnia than men; the difference emerges after puberty, suggesting hormonal causes such as menstruation, pregnancy and menopause.
A longitudinal UK study found 69 per cent of respondents with insomnia at the start still had it 12 months later.

Still Up is an Apple TV+ comedy following best friends Lisa (Antonia Thomas) and Danny (Craig Roberts), who talk late into the night because they can't sleep; Lisa checks into a sleep clinic in London.
Still Up was inspired by creator Natalie Walter's own insomnia and her late-night Facebook chats with co-writer Steve Burge.
Dr Lindsay Browning says insomnia often persists after its trigger is gone, because people start worrying about not sleeping, a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Dr Browning says quick fixes can work like a placebo in the short term, and that vulnerable insomniacs are at risk of being mis-sold expensive products; some clients have spent hundreds of pounds on things that made no difference.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBTI) is described by Dr Browning as the gold standard and a 'complete cure' many people don't know about; it addresses negative thoughts and worries that perpetuate insomnia.
A new drug called Quviviq was approved by the NHS the week before publication; Dr Browning calls it 'exciting' because it acts differently from sleeping pills that cause tolerance.
Amy Fieldhouse-Downes began suffering insomnia after the birth of her second son in 2019 and only found rest after using specialised earplugs.
Rosie Davies-Smith, a PR consultant, spent more than £600 on treatments, and found her true breakthrough came from therapy addressing root causes.
Video producer Preshita found taking a shower before bed and keeping her bedroom clutter-free most effective, and also said masturbation worked.
Jennifer Aniston advises sleeping with her phone at least five feet away, while Martha Stewart recommends focusing on breathing.
